1.0.s.en: (2) The burnt offering from the herd

1.0.0.en: Offering: a gift by which a person draws near to God for the forgiveness of his sin or to give thanks.

1.0.1.en: God begins to speak to Moses, saying that when a person presents any offering, it must be of the clean animals (cattle and sheep). This offering signifies Christ, who became for us a mediator and an eternal sacrifice by which we draw near to the heavenly Father. And because the work of redemption (which belongs to Christ) has many aspects, God appointed for Moses five offerings, four of them animal sacrifices, to make clear the different aspects of this work.

1.0.2.en: The animals suitable for the burnt offering are cattle and sheep: cattle are a symbol of giving, and sheep are a symbol of sacrifice and meekness, and both are attributes of Christ.

1.1.0.en: Burnt offering: a sacrifice that is burned entirely on the altar.

1.1.1.en: Without blemish: having no defect, deformity or disease.

1.1.2.en: Tabernacle of the congregation: this is the church of the Old Testament.

1.1.3.en: This chapter and the chapters that follow mention five kinds of offerings: four of them are sacrifices, and the fifth is a grain offering, that is, an offering of food. These five offerings are:

1.1.8.en: 5- The trespass offering (ch. 5). These five sacrifices mentioned at the beginning of the Book of Leviticus are five aspects of the sacrifice of the Cross, as follows:

1.1.9.en: 1- The burnt offering (ch. 1): in which the whole animal is burned to please God, and it signifies the sacrifice of Christ, who by His death on the Cross pleased the Father.

1.1.10.en: 2- The sin offering (ch. 4, 5): part of which is burned on the altar while the rest is eaten by the priest. It signifies the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, who took away our sins and reconciled us with the Father (1 Pet 2:24). This sacrifice speaks to us of our sins directed toward others, and of course any sin against others is also against God.

1.1.11.en: 3- The trespass offering (ch. 5): in which part is burned on the altar and the rest is eaten by the priest, and it speaks to us of our sins directed toward God directly. It signifies the sacrifice of Christ, who bore all kinds of sins, whether toward God or toward men.

1.1.12.en: 4- The grain offering (ch. 2): in which part is presented on the altar and the rest is eaten by the priest. It signifies the life of Christ in the flesh, in which He fulfilled all righteousness for us (Mt 3:15), and in it He endured many toils throughout His life on earth.

1.1.13.en: 5- The peace offering (ch. 3): in which part is burned on the altar, part is eaten by the priest, and the rest is eaten by the one who offers the sacrifice. It is the only sacrifice of which the one who offers it eats, and so it signifies the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, presented on the altar every day as Body and Blood to be eaten by those who believe in Him. The first of the five sacrifices is called the burnt offering, and it signifies Christ's obedience to the Father on behalf of humanity, and by this the Father was pleased with humanity in Christ. Therefore God is pleased with the one who offers the burnt offering, and it is the only one of the five sacrifices that no one is permitted to offer unless he is a Jew, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb 11:6). And since this sacrifice signifies Christ hanging on the Cross, God stipulated, as a strong indication, that it be a male without blemish.

1.1.14.en: The mention of the herd means the young bull or the full-grown ox, and it signifies spiritual manhood and steadfastness, while its being without blemish signifies that Christ was free of any sin. The slaughter takes place at the door of the tabernacle, as an indication of Christ's crucifixion outside the walls of Jerusalem.

1.1.15.en: The steps of presenting the sacrifice were five:

1.1.16.en: 1- Presenting the animal before the tabernacle of the congregation, that is, before the bronze altar.

1.1.17.en: 2- The one who offers it laying his hand upon it.

1.1.19.en: 4- Sprinkling its blood around the altar.

1.1.20.en: 5- Burning the whole animal on the altar, as in the burnt offering, or a part of it, as in the other sacrifices.

1.1.21.en: The burnt offering was offered by a person for himself, or it was offered for the whole people (Lev 8, 9, 16, 23)... as in:

1.1.22.en: 1- The burnt offering of the morning and the evening and of the Sabbath day.

1.1.23.en: 2- The sacrifice of the Day of Atonement and of the other feasts.

1.1.24.en: 3- The sacrifice of the beginnings of the months.

1.1.25.en: There were also burnt offerings that a person offered for himself in special cases, which are:

1.1.27.en: 2- The cleansing of the one with an issue.

1.1.28.en: All the preceding sacrifices were obligatory, and there were also optional or voluntary sacrifices that a person offered, which are:

1.1.30.en: 2- Freewill offerings (ch. 22:18). There are also voluntary sacrifices that the whole people could offer, as happened in the days of David when the Ark of the Covenant was brought to the city of Zion (2 Sam 6:17), and in the days of Solomon at the dedication of the Temple (1 Kgs 8:4, 5).

1.2.0.en: Atonement: forgiveness and covering of sin.

1.2.1.en: When the one who offers the sacrifice lays his hand on the head of the sacrifice, he declares his connection with it, indeed his union with it. The sacrifice signifies Christ, so when the one who offers it lays his hand on the sacrifice, this signifies his union with Christ, and his sins are transferred to the sacrifice, which signifies Christ. And when the sacrifice that bears the sins of the one who offers it is slaughtered, God is pleased with him. All this is a type of Christ, who bore our sins and died for us on the Cross, so that God is pleased with us when we repent and confess our sins, and in the Sacrament of Confession the priest places the cross on the head of the penitent so that his sins are transferred from his head to the head of Christ, and they are forgiven him and God is pleased with him. And when the one who offers the sacrifice lays his hand on the head of the animal, he confesses his sins, declaring that he deserves death, and by laying on his hand he is united with the animal, so that the animal is slaughtered in his place, and he thereby declares his faith in the redemption of the blood shed for him, which signifies the blood of Christ.

1.3.0.en: The Levites would receive the blood in vessels when the animal was slaughtered, and then the priests would take some of this blood, which represents the life of the animal, and sprinkle it round about the bronze altar.

1.3.1.en: Christ was slaughtered on the Cross, and He was both the Priest and the sacrifice, and His blood, that is, His life which He offered, became an eternal atonement to remove the divine wrath before the throne. The blood is sprinkled in the form of a circle because the circle, which has no beginning and no end, points to the unlimited power of the blood of Christ to make atonement for sin.

1.4.0.en: Flay: to separate the skin from the flesh so that the inside of the sacrifice is exposed.

1.4.1.en: The one who offers the sacrifice flays the skin of the animal after slaughtering it, and then cuts its flesh into pieces at its various joints. The skin is taken by the priest (ch. 7, 8), while the pieces of flesh, which have become exposed after the skin is removed, are laid on the altar.

1.4.2.en: Here it becomes clear that Christ's obedience to the Father was not merely outward but from the depths of His being, and comprehensive of all His members, that is, His actions, and consequently it includes all the members of His Body, that is, we who believe in Him, members of His Church, so that we obey God's commandments. The cutting of the sacrifice into pieces means the exposing of every member in it, so that His obedience is complete from the heart, as we have mentioned, in addition to Christ's endurance of sufferings. And in His likeness the believer endures many toils in his spiritual striving, not only outward torments but also inward pains, because of his love for Christ.

1.5.0.en: Wood: dry fuel of timber that signifies the Cross; these are dry plant sticks.

1.5.1.en: The priests, the sons of Aaron, take of the holy fire that came down from heaven upon the sacrifice on the day of the anointing of Aaron and his sons, and this fire remained burning throughout the days, and with it they kindle the sacrifices. Then the priests bring some sticks of wood and kindle the fire with them so that it burns.

1.5.2.en: The fire signifies Christ's love for the Father, which reached its summit on the wood of the Cross on which He offered Himself as a sacrifice of obedience to the Father, for the fire shows the fierce sufferings that Christ endured for our sake. The Church portrays this scene when the priest holds the three candles on the cross in the prayer "God, have mercy on us" during the raising of incense, as a reference to the crucified Christ, one of the three hypostases, who brought God's mercy to the believers, removed His wrath from them, and illumined the world with His salvation.

1.6.0.en: Lay in order: they place the pieces of the sacrifice beside one another to give the shape of the whole animal.

1.6.1.en: The head is Christ and the pieces are we, and the fat is the best of the richness of the sacrifice, that is, the divine attributes and perfections of Christ, which make atonement for His children by His work of redemption, and the priests, by their authority, convey them to the believers through the Sacraments by the work of the fiery Holy Spirit.

1.7.0.en: Inwards: what is inside the sacrifice.

1.7.2.en: Offering made by fire: an offering to God burned with fire.

1.7.3.en: The priest washes the inside and the inwards of the animal three times, as the scholars of the Jews say, and this signifies purity of heart, and he washes the legs as a symbol of purity of conduct, and then he burns it all with fire, and God is pleased with this love offered to Him, since it is an offering of love and not an atonement for a particular sin. Therefore the burnt offering is distinguished by the phrase "a sweet savour," just as God was pleased with the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross.

1.7.4.en: The washing with water signifies Baptism, which transfers to us the work of Christ's obedience to the Father so that our depths are cleansed by it and our conduct and nature are changed, so that the righteousness of Christ covers us and the Father is pleased with us and delights in us.

1.7.5.en: If the Holy Christ offered perfect obedience to the Father, how fitting it is for me to offer my obedience and submission as a sacrifice of love to Christ in return for His love for me, so that I obey His commandments even if they are difficult, and trust that God will support me.

1.8.s.en: (3) The burnt offering from the flock

1.8.1.en: Those who are not financially able may offer the burnt offering from the flock with the same ritual as before, and it is slaughtered on the right side of the altar, the side facing north (because the front of the altar faces west), because Christ's obedience to the Father brought the Father's good pleasure upon us in Christ, so that we sit at His right side, enjoying His favor. In the burnt offering of sheep everything that was said before about the burnt offering of cattle is to be observed, so it is to be a male without blemish, and after it is slaughtered its blood is sprinkled around the altar, and it is cut up and burned on the altar in the same way mentioned before for the burnt offering of cattle.

1.8.2.en: If you are not able to offer God many gifts, then offer according to your ability, even if it is something small, and trust that your gifts and your labor are very precious to God, however small, and may even be more precious in His eyes than the large gifts offered by the rich, just as He rejoiced in the widow's two mites and glorified her more than all.

1.9.s.en: (4) The burnt offering from the birds

1.9.0.en: Turtledoves: a kind of wild dove.

1.9.2.en: Wring off: to split it around without separating it.

1.9.4.en: Feathers: the waste of food in the belly.

1.9.5.en: Ashes: the remains of the burning.

1.9.6.en: Cleave it with the wings thereof: it was the ancient custom, when a covenant was made between two parties, that the sacrifices were split and one half placed on the right and the other half on the left, and the two parties to the covenant passed between the two halves of the split sacrifice. This signifies the covenant that the one who offers the sacrifice makes with God, by repentance and living for Him. This is the burnt offering for the one who is not financially able to offer what was mentioned before, because even the poor raise birds in their homes. The ritual of the sacrifice is as before, with the throwing of the food and its waste in the place of the ashes, because material foods are destined to perish. And the splitting of the sacrifice is a declaration of the covenant with God, but without separating it, because not a bone of Christ would be broken; He bore our sins, yet He is without sin. The turtledove is a clean bird because the Christian shrinks from sin, while the young pigeon represents meekness and humility. The flesh of the turtledove, whether young or old, is palatable, whereas of the pigeon only the young is palatable, and so God accepts the best thing, which is young pigeons. It is noted that the head of the bird is wrung off and the bird is split down the middle between the wings over the altar, because its blood is little, so the priest squeezes it out on the side of the altar.

1.9.7.en: The offering of birds as sacrifices to God was known from ancient times, for Noah offered some of them to God (Gen 8:20), and so did our father Abraham (Gen 15:9).

1.9.8.en: I hope that you will review the meekness of your character and your aversion to sin as a pure son of Christ, so that you do not mix with the wicked or sit in places that do not befit the children of God, and if you fall into sin, hasten to repentance to regain your purity.

1.9.9.en: The grain offering. The second aspect of the sacrifice of the Cross, which the grain offering makes clear, is the pure humanity of the Lord and the wonderful mystery of His Incarnation. This offering is made of wheat in the form of flour baked in different ways.

2.0.s.en: (1) The grain offering in the form of fine flour

2.0.3.en: Drawing near to God here is by an offering of fine flour, from which bread is made, for Christ is the source of our satisfaction because He is the bread of life, and He is the only mediator between God and men by His redeeming person and His atoning intercession. Olive oil represents the Holy Spirit, who softens the heart and lights its lamp with light and grants it peace, like the dove that came to give Noah the good news of the return of peace to the earth, with the olive branch that it carried to him. As for frankincense, it points to the prayer and worship that are offered wholly to God alone.

2.1.0.en: The priest takes a handful of the flour with the oil poured on it, together with all the frankincense, and lays it on the altar to be burned on it. It signifies Christ, who lived a pure life on earth to teach us how to walk in our lives, and then died on the Cross for us. The flour signifies the life of Christ in the flesh on earth, the oil the Holy Spirit who anointed Him, and the incense His worship and prayers; that is, the grain offering means Christ's purity in the flesh and His perfection in fulfilling all righteousness for us.

2.2.0.en: Most holy: eaten by the priests only.

2.2.1.en: The priests, that is, Aaron and his sons, eat the remainder of the grain offering in the house of the Lord, because this offering is most holy to the Lord, that is, it is eaten in His house, and likewise the showbread (Ex 35:13; ch. 24:9) and the portions of the priests from the sin offering (ch. 7:1-10; 14:13). There were some offerings that were considered holy and were eaten by the priest and his family in a clean place and not in the house of the Lord, as in the eating of the peace offerings (Num 6:20). The priest's eating of the grain offering declares:

2.2.2.en: 1- God's acceptance of the offering, since His priests eat it.

2.2.3.en: 2- The grace given to the priests to carry out their pastoral responsibilities and the service of God.

2.2.4.en: 3- God's care for the needs of the priests and His children who are consecrated to His service and who have left the material works of the world.

2.2.5.en: Your whole life belongs to God, so take care to offer sufficient time for worship and service, like the handful of flour offered on the altar, and God will rejoice in you and bless all your works.

2.3.s.en: (2) The grain offering in the form of baked things

2.3.4.en: The other kind of grain offering is what is baked inside the oven, and it is of two kinds:

2.3.5.en: 1- Flour kneaded with water and oil and made in the form of cakes without putting in leaven, because leaven signifies evil.

2.3.6.en: 2- Flour kneaded with water and made in the form of wafers and then anointed with oil, and no leaven is put in them either, but they are unleavened.

2.3.7.en: The baked things signify Christ, who passed through sufferings for our salvation. He was conceived of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin and was anointed with the Holy Spirit who descended upon Him at His baptism, and the Holy Spirit is signified by the oil with which the baked things are anointed, to declare the setting apart of His gentle, pure person, free from sin, to accomplish salvation and redemption. The unleavened bread, free of leaven, signifies the life of Christ, pure of evil, for the flour signifies the humanity of Christ and the oil the Holy Spirit.

2.4.0.en: Baking pan: a metal disc on which the baked things are placed in the oven to be done.

2.4.1.en: Part it in pieces: to break it into small parts.

2.4.2.en: The third kind of baked things is flour kneaded with water and oil and made in the form of wafers that are placed on a baking pan and put into the oven, and after they are done they are left to cool and dry, and then they are broken into small pieces and oil is poured on them. This signifies the life of Christ on earth, which was pure in all its details, for the breaking of the wafers is like the cutting of the sacrifice into pieces to show that its inside is pure.

2.4.3.en: Have you accustomed yourself to examine the details of your daily conduct before God to make sure of its purity, and to repent of your sins? For the deceiver, the devil, tries to slip in some impure little thoughts or works, so as to corrupt your heart and bring you down to greater errors. So be careful and examine yourself every day, and seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit in prayer and the counsel of your father of confession.

2.5.s.en: (3) The grain offering in the form of dough in a frying pan

2.5.0.en: Frying pan: a deep earthen vessel.

2.5.1.en: Another kind of baked things is flour kneaded with oil and put in a frying pan and cooked in it. The pan signifies the body of the Virgin, which appears like the body of an ordinary person, and the clay signifies it, but it received great honor through the birth of Christ from it, whom the flour kneaded with oil signifies.

2.6.0.en: The priest takes a part of the flour kneaded with oil in the pan and lays it on the altar to be burned on it, and God is pleased with it as He was pleased with the sacrifice of His only-begotten Son, who lived a pure life on earth and offered Himself as a ransom for us on the Cross.

2.7.0.en: The remainder of the dough baked in the pan is eaten by the holy priests who are set apart for the service of God, and this declares God's special blessing for the priests, His servants, by which they are able to serve Him and to bind the people to the love of God.

2.7.1.en: If you serve God, know that He will give you special help and blessing to carry out His service, and in proportion to what you give in service you will receive greater help, so that you enjoy the vision of God in your life and rejoice in His work in others.

2.8.s.en: (4) General conditions for the grain offering

2.8.0.en: God forbids the putting of leaven or honey into the grain offerings, for leaven in dough signifies the evil that works secretly in a person's heart, and honey signifies the sin that a person insists on loving, which is in his eyes as sweet as honey. This spoils a person's offerings to God, that is, God does not accept them.

2.9.0.en: Oblation of the firstfruits: the offering of the firstfruits, which is the first produce of the crops or of the agricultural or animal products.

2.9.1.en: It is permissible to offer the firstfruits to the Lord even if they are of leaven or honey, because they are used as food for the servants of the altar, but it is not permissible to offer them as an offering on the altar of the Lord so that the Lord may be pleased with the one who offers it; that is, they are given to the priest and he eats of them. This is a divine declaration that leavened bread and honey are not unclean, but they signify the spiritual meanings mentioned before, so they are not offered on the altar, but a person eats them with thanksgiving from the hand of God.

2.10.0.en: When you offer any offering to the Lord, you are to put salt on it, because salt preserves from corruption, so the offering with salt on it points to the humanity of Christ, which did not see corruption.

2.10.1.en: And the putting of salt on the offering signifies the covenant with God, since the ancients were accustomed, when making treaties, to eat bread and salt, in addition to the fact that salt makes food palatable.

2.10.2.en: Do not be deceived by the sweetness of sin, for it carries within it the poison of death, so keep away from everything that stirs desire, whether by sight or hearing or any other form, so that you keep yourself pure.

2.11.s.en: (5) The offering of the firstfruits of wheat in the form of green ears

2.11.0.en: Green ears: green wheat that has not fully ripened.

2.11.3.en: When the firstfruits of the wheat crop are offered to the Lord, they are to be of green ears of wheat roasted with fire, as a reference to the sufferings of Christ, who called Himself the grain of wheat, and who bore the fire of suffering and crushing in His crucifixion. The firstfruits may also be offered from wheat that is crushed and broken or from what is pounded fine. The Holy Bible mentions the offering of the firstfruits in detail in (ch. 23:9-21, 33-36), (Ex 23:14-19), (Deut 16:13-17).
